title: Mexico Is a Leader in the Fight Against Hunger, United Nations Praises
author: Alexia Villaseñor and Jared Laureles
content:
_This article by[Alexia Villaseñor and Jared
Laureles](https://www.jornada.com.mx/autores/Alexia%20Villase%C3%B1or%20y%20Jared%20Laureles)
originally appeared in the [October 5, 2026 edition of La
Jornada](https://www.jornada.com.mx/noticia/2026/10/05/sociedad/mexico-es-
lider-en-el-combate-al-hambre-elogia-naciones-unidas), Mexico's premier left
wing daily newspaper._

Amid a global scenario in which acute hunger has reached record levels, with
**300 million people affected** , Mexico plays a leadership role and its
policies to combat poverty and improve nutrition are experiences that other
countries can draw on, said Carl Skau, acting executive director of the United
Nations World Food Programme (WFP).

In an interview with _La Jornada_ , he highlighted the social programs and the
nutritious school breakfasts (in their cold and hot modalities), as well as
the model of local purchases directly from small producers. He also
highlighted the regulation of products sold in schools and front-of-package
labeling, measures about which he warned: "there are many forces against
them."

This recognition of the Mexican model comes in a context of growing
deterioration of global food security. As the official detailed, between 2020
and 2025 the number of people with acute hunger **tripled** –going from 100
million to 300 million– due to wars, disruptions to maritime trade (such as
those in the Strait of Hormuz) and climate change. On this last point, he
warned that the effects of the El Niño phenomenon could prolong the food
crisis for up to 18 months, especially in the poorest and most marginalized
areas.

![A hand ladles food into a plastic bag held out by another person at a
community food distribution.](https://mexicosolidarity.com/wp-
content/uploads/2026/10/2026-10-05-mexico-leader-hunger-un-02-food-
aid.jpg)Between 2020 and 2025 the number of people with acute hunger tripled,
going from 100 million to 300 million, due to wars, disruptions to maritime
trade (such as those in the Strait of Hormuz) and climate change. Photo: AFP

Latin America and the Caribbean are already feeling this situation. Although
the region is one of the world's main food suppliers, 41 million people still
suffer from hunger and it has the highest cost on the planet for accessing a
healthy diet; only one in four people can afford it. The challenge is no
longer only to produce food, but to guarantee access to nutritious products,
he said.

Skau, with more than 25 years of experience in diplomacy and humanitarian
affairs, visited Mexico last week to strengthen dialogue with local
authorities around shared priorities, and highlighted the country's role in
promoting multilateral solutions to an increasingly complex food crisis.

Among the Mexican experiences he considered relevant is school feeding. "On
this issue (Mexico) has a leadership role, because they started working early
on school feeding," he emphasized.

The programs include daily breakfasts with milk, cereals and fruit; in full-
time schools, a hot meal is also offered, prioritizing vegetables, proteins,
plain water and tortillas, while the dishes are prepared with little oil and
no added sugars.

The acting WFP director also highlighted the participation of communities,
particularly of women in school kitchens, since, in addition to preserving the
habits and traditional food of each region –he explained–, they find in those
spaces a source of work without needing to leave their places of origin.

> A country that is carrying out domestic public policies aimed at combating
> hunger, to promote good-quality, healthy food, is relevant to us, and we
> take it to other countries that need similar policies. The example of Mexico
> is very important.
>
> Carl Skau, acting executive director of the World Food Programme

Some of these experiences have already begun to be transferred to other
nations in the region, such as **Colombia and Peru**. The mechanism consists
of organizing learning missions and workshops of several days, in which
specialists from one country share their experiences with officials and
experts from another, he said.

During his meetings with the Secretary of Foreign Relations, Roberto Velasco,
as well as with authorities from the Secretariat of Health, Skau specified
that areas of collaboration were identified to promote a common agenda in
regional and global spaces such as the Community of Latin American and
Caribbean States (Celac), the G20 and the United Nations.

He warned that international organizations lack sufficient resources to
address the current humanitarian crises; the WFP has **lost 40 percent of its
budget** in the past two years, some 4 billion dollars.

For this reason, he stressed, the relationship between Mexico and the WFP
focuses on technical cooperation, knowledge exchange and the strengthening of
public policies. In addition, the country provides grains, legumes and other
essential foods for the organization's humanitarian assistance operations in
emergencies in different parts of the world.
